document.title: Purification and Some Properties of Tobacco Streak and Tulare
document.abstract: ROBERT IV. I:UI,TOX Tobacco streak virus (TS1-) was stabilized in ext,racts by P-mercaptoethanol and, after clarification of the ext)racts with hydrated calcium phosphate, concentrated by high speed centrifugation.

There were several reasons for developing a purification method for tobacco streak virus (TSV). The virus is unstable in crude extracts and apparently is permanently inactivated by oxidized phenolic compounds (Fulton, 1949) in tissue extracts. Inactivation can be prevented by antioxidants, which should make it' possible to retain infectivity while separating the virus from deleterious tissue components. Purified virus, if relatively stable, would provide favorable mat'erial for investigating t)he nature of the inactivation in tissue extracts.
Another reason for attempting purification of TSV was that in preliminary trials of several plant species as local lesion assay hosts, the dilution infectivity curves obtained wit,h some hosts were abnormally steep and resembled those reported for t,wo Prunus viruses (Fulton, 1962). TSV offers some advantages over the stone fruit viruses for investigating the nature of such multiplehit dilution curves. The infectivity of extracts of TSV-infected tobacco tissue suggested that they contained more virus than could be obtained in tissue infected with stone fruit viruses. TSV also exists in a number of st'rains that, produce dist,inctive symptoms on tobacco and other hosts.
TSV has been recorded from a wide variety of plants and from widely scattered locations (Costa and Carvalho, 1961;Patino and Zaumeyer, 1959;Devergne, 1961;Thomas and Zaumeyer, 1950). Antiserum produced from purified virus would be useful for ident'ifying suspected isolates. Scott, et al. (1961) prepared an anGserum to the bean red node strain of TSV with virus partially purified by chloroform-butanol extraction and alternating high and low speed centrifugation. The antiserum, however, had a fairly high titer of antibody to host protein. Mink et ab. (1966) purified the bean red node strain of TSV from bean stem tissue by means of a charcoal-freezing process. The method, however, was reported as leaving pigment in preparations from leaf tissue. Aft,er an effective purification method had been developed for TSV, it was applied to Tulare apple mosaic virus (TAiW), which has many properties similar to TSV (31ink et al., 1963).
Three isolates of TSV originally were found in tobacco. These ranged in severit) on tobacco from typical (strain HI;), to medium (McO,to mild (11). One isolate (WC) was obtained from white clover. Another isolate (DV) was one of several obt'ained from naturally infected IMlia variubilis (Willd.) Desf. and reproduced t,he original chlorotic bands and rings when inoculated to Feedlings of this plant. The bean red node strain wax obtained from WI. ,J. Zaumeyer. Tulare apple mosuic virus was obt'ained from C. E. Yarwood. All isolat,es were kept in diced tobacco tissue that, had been dehydrated cold in a vacuum. Some such preparations of TSV have remained infect,ive for over 18 years at, 2-4".

After midribs were removed, infect,ed leaves were chilled and homogenized in cold phosphat,e buffer in a Waring Hlcndor for 5 minutes. Antifoam A (Dow-Corning) was added to prevent' foaming. The proportion (by weight) of leaves to buffer, and the concentration of buffer affected t,he degree of clarification obtained. A volume of 0.02 3, pH S.0 buffer equivalent to 1.5 times the weight, of tissue was most satisfactory.
To stabilize infectivity, 2-ME was added to the buffer, before t'he leaves were homogenized, to make an 0.02 M solution. Although sodium diethyldithiocarbamate did not stabilize infectivity, it was also added to the buffer to make 0.02 ill. Without it t,he virus pellets were brown.
The leaf homogenat,e was centrifuged in 250-ml bottles for 20 minutes at 3000 rpm in an International model UV centrifuge. The supernatant liquid was then stirred 3 minutes with a volume of HCP equivalent to 0.S of the original weight of tissue. When tissue was rather necrotic, or when an 0.8 portion failed to clarify the extract completely, an additional portion (0.1 of the tissue weight) was used. This mixture was centrifuged 20 minutes at 3000 rpm.
The clear yelIow supernat,ant liquid from the HCP clarification was centrifuged 2.5 hours at 30,000 rpm in a Spinco No. 30 rotor. The resulting pellets were resuspended in 0.02 M phosphate buffer, pH S.0, by shaking on a mechanical shaker at 2". The volume for resuspension was as small as practical, usually 0.5 ml per tube.
The resuspended pellets were centrifuged for 20 minutes at 10,000 rpm in a Spinco No. 40 rotor. This removed some of the insoluble mat'erial. The supernatant liquid contained the virus and appreciable amounts of host protein, not all of which was removed by subsequent cycles of high and low speed centrifugation.
Other methods were tried, therefore, in attempts to remove this extraneous material.
Acidification of the resuspended pellets to pH 5.2 with HCI, HSPOJ, or citric acid was fairlv effective. The virus withstood the acidity for the t,ime required t'o remove the precipitate by centrifugation.
Contaminating material was not completely removed, but acidification wit,h citric acid was used with many preparations to simplify subsequent purification steps.
Heating the resuspended pellets t'o 38" for 75 minutes or adding 165 mg (NHJSOh per milliliter also precipitated extraneous material and left, the virus in the supernatant liquid. Neither treatment, however, removed all the contaminating protein. Magnesium-saturated bentonite (Dunn and Hitchborn, 1965), with several concentrations of magnesium ion, adsorbed the virus.
Nonvirus material was most efficiently removed by precipitating it with the yglobulin portion of an antiserum prepared with tobacco protein. The procedure was modified slightly from t'hat' described by Gold (1961).

To detect inhomogeneity in purified preparations of TSV, appropriate dilutions were layered on gradients of lo-40 % sucrose in 0.02 M borate buffer, pH 8.0. Gradients were prepared with a modification of an apparatus described by ). After centrifugation in a Spinco SW 23.1 rotor, contents of the tubes were scanned with an ISCO density gradient fractionator (Instrumentation Specialties Co., Lincoln, Nebraska)

Preparations centrifuged 3 hours or longer at 25,000 rpm in 0.02 M borate buffer, pH S.0, showed two closely spaced, but distinct, zones. When purified preparations of TSV were run in a Spinco model E analytical centrifuge, the two components had sedimentation coefficients of about 72 S and 96 S. Because they were closely spaced, samples were taken from the upper half of the upper zone and the lower half of the lower zone in density gradient tubes. Only samples from the lower zone were infectious.
The UV absorpt,ion curves were similar for each zone. The A260:280 ratio for the upper zone was 1.49 & 0.06; the ratio for t,he lower zone was 1.53 f 0.06.
Approximately the same scanning patt)ern was found for several different preparations of the HF strain of TSV, with the upper (noninfectious) zone in lower concentration than the lower zone. Other strains were purified and subjected to density gradient centrifugation to see whether the same pattern was characteristic of all strains of the virus.
The proportions of the two components differed among the strains (Fig. 3). For each strain at least one other scanning pattern was obtained on a separate preparat'ion of virus, and only minor differences were found in patterns for any one strain. Preparations of most strains contained less upper component than strain HF. Strain hl, however, was unusual in producing more of the noninfectious upper component' than of the lower component.
Strain iJl was used to investigate some factors that might influence the proportion of the two components. The temperature of incubation of inoculated plants or the host in which the virus was produced did not greatly affect the proportion of the two components (Fig. 4). Upper, symptomless leaves of plants infected for about 6 weeks yielded a preparation with only slightly less of the noninfectious component than a preparation from plants incubated for only a few days (Fig. 4) after inoculation. Storage of purified virus for several months at 2" did not alt'er the proportions of t'he two components, although as much as one-third of the t,otal material was removed as an insoluble, denatured precipitate.

Purified preparations for electron microscopy were fixed with 1% glutaraldehyde for 5-10 minutes and then mixed with an equal volume of 2% PTA. Drops applied to carbon-coated Formvar films were drawn off within a few seconds. Negatively stained TAMV was spherical and somewhat larger than TSV. Most particles were 32-34 rnp in diameter. About 0.3.5 % of the particles were about twice as long as wide (Fig. 6).
With both TSV and TAMV the difficulty in preparing undisrupted virus for electron microscopy suggested t,hat the protein coat of the virus was fragile. Possibly the instability o!' t,he viruses in tissue extracts is related to coat fragility. Both viruses are also relatively urlsbable when purified. Mink et nl. (1966) number of zones obtained when the bean red node strain of TSV was subjected to density gradient, centrifugation depended on the length of time plants had been infected. Preparations from plants infected 4 weeks separated into four zones. Infectivity was associated with the two more rapidly sedimenting zones, with sedimentation coefficients of 103 S and 123 S. These figures are appreciably higher than those found for TSV in this work, and only t'wo components were found in preparatons of each of six strains of TSV. Neither the host species, tobacco or cucumber, or the length of time tobacco was infected significantly affected the proportions of each component. (1966) do not, occur in t'obacco or cucumber, or whether they were selectively removed during purification.
There are a number of examples, as discussed by Schneider and Diener (1966), of viruses t,hat are accompanied by similar particles that sediment more slowly in density gradient centrifugation and that are not infectious. These contain less nucleic acid than t,he infect'ious particles. Judging from the ratios of TiV absorbance at 260 and 2S0 rnp, the two types of TSV particles contain nearly the same amounts of nucleic acid.
